method: No source gives any of the fifteen hazards as a function of the date of full automation. Forecasts conditional on timelines exist only for existential catastrophe (a 2022 LessWrong thread of about 45 forecasters, Metaculus question 12840, Greenblatt's risk by lead time, MacAskill and Taylor's 2026 note) and, weakly, for catastrophe and cybercrime under rapid against slow progress (FRI LEAP wave 9). Every hazard factor is therefore a guess, built in four steps. (1) Reference. The five research files anchor their transition rates on forecasts and defences of 2026 to 2028 and on AGI in about 2027 to 2030; taking 2028.5 and adding about 3.5 years from AGI to full automation gives 2032, five years from the start of 2027. (2) Shorter leads. Factor = compression (the same transition squeezed into fewer years: about 3 at one year, 1.6 at three) x unpreparedness (how much less defence there is than at the reference: 1.05 to 1.3) x lag (the time attackers, strikers, armies and crises need to act: 0.35 to 0.8 at one year). (3) Longer leads. Factor = dilution (a slower takeoff spreads the transition over more than the model's five turbulent years: about 0.9, 0.78, 0.65 and 0.57 at 8, 12, 20 and 30 years) x preparedness (what the extra years buy, hazard by hazard, from the adaptation speeds in the evidence), down to a floor for risk that comes from the capability itself or from states' choices. Where more lead could make things worse (a longer arms race, China at parity, more years of misuse-capable models, a larger debt boom) the high end stays at or above 1. (4) After automation. With a lead under five years the years after automation still lie inside what the old research called the transition, so I give afterFactors above 1 at one and three years that put the rate about 40% and 15% of the way from the after rate to the transition rate, computed on averaged rates so that the product never exceeds the transition rate in any place; from five years on they are 1. Existential catastrophe differs: its factors are derived from the conditional forecasts, and because the existing 0.2 rests on older statements by people with longer timelines I set its factor to 1 at eight years, not five. Low and high values are my 5th and 95th percentiles; the model draws them together with the sceptic-to-concerned spread, so the low end is the view that defenders adapt quickly given time and the high end the view that lead time does not help. Pages were read through a fetch tool that summarises and caps quotations at about 125 characters; the NIST and White House documents were read as PDF text and pages.

turbulentYears.basis: The old window was the five years from AGI; the new one ends at full automation. AGI to full automation is about 3.5 years on central views (2 to 2.5 in the race ending of AI 2027, https://ai-2027.com/race; 2.8 between Metaculus's weak and strong AGI medians, 11 Aug 2027 and 23 May 2030; about 3 from 20% to 100% of cognitive tasks in Davidson 2023; a decade or more on slow views), so a five-year window ending at automation starts about a year before AGI, where ai-timelines.md already puts misuse and economic risk. I keep five so that the existing yearly figures cover the same number of years. Lo: fast takeoff. Hi: slow diffusion. The true length grows with the lead time; the factors carry that as dilution.

runUpYears.basis: The excess is visible well before AGI: today's cyber rates are already 2 to 10 times baseline and the first AI-run intrusions date from 2025 (research/ai/ai-cyber.md), about three years before a turbulent period that starts in 2027 or 2028 on the reference view. Davidson's median of about 3 years from 20% to 100% automation of cognitive tasks gives the same length for partial automation (https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/Gc9FGtdXhK9sCSEYu/what-a-compute-centric-framework-says-about-ai-takeoff). Lo: war and coup risk, which arrive with AGI. Hi: labour-market and fraud effects on slow-diffusion views.

referenceLeadYears.basis: Inferred from the five files. Their transition rates lean on forecasts and defences of 2026 to 2028 (FRI's biorisk conditionals for 2028, the FRI and GovAI grid pilot for 2026, Sentinel's forecasts for 2028, the Fed's 2026 AI-debt figures, Metaculus war questions to 2035) and on AGI in about 2027 to 2030 (ai-timelines.md: the weighted centre moved to 2027-2029 in November 2026; Metaculus strong AGI 2030). Centre 2028.5, plus about 3.5 years to full automation, is 2032: five years from the start of 2027. By hazard: cyber and bio 4 to 5, economy 5 to 6, war 5 to 7. The existential figure of 0.2 fits a lead of 8 to 12 years and is treated separately.

pandemicModerate.mechanism: The transition excess is small (2.2% to 2.8% a year) and comes from human-caused releases once AI clears the remaining capability thresholds and automated laboratories remove the wet-lab bottleneck, net of better detection of natural outbreaks. Preparation that takes time: verifiable screening of synthesis orders and benchtop synthesisers (sixteen years, by my recollection of the first guidance in 2010, to a policy that binds only federally funded buyers, with 250 to 340 days more to implement), vaccine platforms (326 days for the first COVID-19 vaccines against a goal of 100), and stockpiles, detection and clean air on the ten-year scale of the Apollo programme for biodefense. With little lead none of it is in place, but a release takes months of physical work and an epidemic months to spread, so the yearly rate rises less than for software hazards. With a long lead the excess falls slowly and not to zero: state programmes and laboratory accidents are untouched by screening, biotechnology itself advances, and more years pass in which capable open models exist (the model counts those years at today's rate). Floor assumed: 0.4 at 30 years.

evidence.claim: FRI (1 July 2025, revised 30 April 2026): the median expert put a human-caused epidemic of 100,000 deaths in 2028 at 0.3% a year, 1.5% conditional on several LLM capabilities, and 'close to baseline (0.4%)' when strict model safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening are adopted (from 1.25% in the scenario tested).

White House memorandum NSTM-6, 5 November 2026: the National Policy for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening 'requires all recipients of Federal life sciences funding to procure synthetic nucleic acids and benchtop synthesis equipment exclusively from certified suppliers'; NIST standards within 90 days, first list of adherent suppliers within 160 days, procurement from certified suppliers within 250 days and benchtop equipment within 340 days. It replaces the 2024 Framework and, on full implementation, the 2023 HHS guidance; 'Existing Federal guidance has relied on self-attestation'.

CEPI: the 100 Days Mission 'aims to develop safe, effective and accessible vaccines within 100 days of identifying a new pandemic threat'; for COVID-19, 'Within just 326 days, the first safe and effective vaccines were being rolled out.'

Bipartisan Commission on Biodefense, January 2021: the Apollo Program for Biodefense 'could effectively end the era of pandemic threats by 2030'; 'Even the most ambitious program (about $10 billion annually) would be a small fraction of the current cost'. A ten-year programme, proposed and not funded at that scale (the last clause is my recollection).

That the first federal screening guidance dates from 2010 is my recollection; the White House memorandum names only the 2023 HHS guidance and the 2024 Framework. pandemicSevere.mechanism: As for pandemicModerate, but the excess is larger (0.4% to 1.5% a year) and comes mostly from deliberate releases selected for severity. FRI's experts put the yearly chance of a human-caused epidemic at 0.3%, at 1.5% once several AI capabilities exist, and back near baseline (0.4%) with strict model safeguards and legally mandatory synthesis screening. So the part of the excess due to lone actors is removable, and what it takes is regulation, which has moved slowly: guidance in 2010 (my recollection), a revision in 2023, a framework in 2024, and in November 2026 a policy for federally funded buyers only. Detection, rapid vaccines, protective equipment and clean air need about a decade of funded work. A short lead leaves 2026 defences facing full capability, tempered by the months a release takes. A long lead helps less than in cyber: one success suffices, states and accidents lie outside screening, and Esvelt and Amodei argue that biology favours attack (ai-bio.md). More lead also means more years of misuse-capable models before automation, which the model counts at today's rate. Floor assumed: 0.42 at 30 years.

evidence.claim: FRI: median expert 0.3% a year for a human-caused epidemic in 2028; 'rose to 1.5% conditional on several hypothetical LLM capabilities'; 2.3% with capabilities combined; experts 'reduced their risk forecast close to baseline (0.4%)' with LLM safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening. cyberOutage.mechanism: The transition rate is driven by attacks on grid control systems by whoever holds an unsafeguarded AGI-level model, by state sabotage of data centres and their power supply during the race, and by accidents in AI-run operations. Preparation that takes time: control equipment is replaced on a 10-to-15-year cycle against 3 to 5 for office IT, so hardening comes through segmentation and monitoring in years and through replacement in decades; moving data centres onto their own generation takes years; restraint on attacking civilian infrastructure needs agreements of the kind that took decades for nuclear weapons. A short lead compresses the race, so that sabotage and access already held (at least five years for Volt Typhoon, per CISA in ai-cyber.md) are used against today's grid. A long lead lets utilities harden and spreads the transition, but more AI load sits on shared grids, and state sabotage is a decision, not a vulnerability. Floor assumed: 0.35 at 30 years.

gridLong.mechanism: A grid failure of weeks needs physical damage to long-lead equipment or an attacker able to defeat many restorations at once (GovAI, in ai-cyber.md); the transition figure adds escalation to kinetic attack on data centres and power plants. None of this can be done in one to three years, and the escalation route is strongest in the most compressed race. With a long lead, spares and hardening accumulate, but the physical route is tied to war risk, which falls slowly. Floor assumed: 0.38 at 30 years.

waterSystemFailure.mechanism: Water is the softest utility: tens of thousands of small systems, old controllers reachable from the internet, no security staff (ai-cyber.md). paymentsOutage.mechanism: Payments are software, concentrated in a few processors, and the transition figure assumes AGI-level offence in many hands against today's estates. Exploitation now begins on average seven days before a patch exists; the median organisation takes 43 days to patch and fully fixes 26% of known-exploited flaws; and in June 2026 Anthropic expected Mythos-class models at many companies within 6 to 12 months. Defence can catch up, and finance is the best-resourced and most regulated defender: flaws found by AI can be fixed before attackers find them, new code can be written memory-safe (Android cut the memory-safety share of its vulnerabilities from 76% in 2019 to an expected 24% in 2024), and resilience rules take a few years to adopt and apply (the EU's DORA: regulation of December 2022, binding from January 2025). So this is the hazard where lead time helps most: I take the excess to fall by a third with three more years and by 60% with seven. A short lead does the reverse. Floor assumed: 0.2 at 30 years, for state attack on finance, concentration, and failures caused by AI-run operations and rushed patching.

bankingCrisis.mechanism: The transition figure rests on a jump in real interest rates, runs made faster by AI agents, erosion of the tax base and the bust of a debt-financed AI boom. Speed matters in the record: after three years of rapid growth in credit and asset prices the chance of a crisis within three years is about 40%, against 7% in normal times. A faster transition means a faster boom, a sharper repricing and no time for supervisors, whose rule-making runs on a ten-year clock (Basel III: published 2010, final reforms endorsed 2017, transitional arrangements to 2028). A slower one lets balance sheets, rate expectations and rules adjust. Two things limit the gain: rates must reprice however long the wait, and with a long lead the AI boom of 2026 may bust first because AI came slower than priced, a risk that falls in the next few years and that this factor does not capture. A crisis also takes a year or more to brew, which tempers the factor at one year and moves part of it after automation. Floor assumed: 0.4 at 30 years.

greatPowerWar.mechanism: The transition figure triples the US-China rate for preventive attack, sabotage that escalates, and Taiwan's place in chip supply. Theory makes speed the cause: Powell shows that large, rapid shifts in the distribution of power can lead to war, because the rising side cannot commit to restraint; a slower shift leaves room for bargains. Time also allows agreements, though slowly: SALT I took two and a half years of talks and came 27 years after the first bomb, and the non-proliferation treaty took seven years from proposal to signature. Against this, a longer lead means a longer arms race, and MacAskill and Taylor put China's chance of a decisive advantage at 10%, 30% and 50% on short, medium and long timelines: a contest between near-equals in place of a US lead, though RAND finds preventive attack relatively more likely where one side has a monopoly to preserve. I take the excess to fall slowly, with a high floor of 0.5 at 30 years and an upper bound above 1. At a one-year lead the shift is largest, but wars take time to decide and mobilise, and one side may prevail before the other can act.

existential.mechanism: The chance of existential catastrophe given AGI is the one figure for which forecasts by arrival date exist, and all point the same way. In a 2022 thread about 45 forecasters gave it for five arrival windows; their medians fall from 74% (2025 to 2030) to 65% (2030 to 2040), 46% (2040 to 2060) and 34.5% (after 2060), and none of the thirteen named forecasters I checked rises from the second window on. Metaculus shows 30% for arrival in 2030 to 2039 against 11% for 2060 to 2099. Greenblatt's estimates of takeover fall from 45% with no lead for safety work to 20% with months, 13% with one to three years and 7% with ten. The mechanisms: more years of alignment and control research, with more capable assistants and more warning, and a slower takeoff (MacAskill and Taylor; Davidson); against them, a compute overhang that could make a late takeoff very fast (Kokotajlo), and less influence for those now working on the problem. The existing figure of 0.2 comes from statements of 2020 to 2024 by people whose median AGI dates were then in the 2030s and 2040s, so I set the factor to 1 at eight years, not five; at five it is 1.15. Floor assumed: 0.57 at 30 years. The forecasts for arrival after 2060 go lower (0.3 to 0.5 of the 2025-2030 level) but lie beyond the table. A multiplier on a probability misbehaves near 1: for the highly concerned view (0.8) any factor above 1.25 is capped.

openQuestions: The five-year average is not monotonic in the year. With these figures the shift for most hazards peaks for automation around 2031 to 2032, when all five years of the horizon are turbulent, and is lower for 2028 or 2029, when most of the horizon lies after automation. The yearly rate before automation does rise the sooner it comes. How much lower depends on the afterFactors at one and three years, which are my weakest guesses; the existential factor works the other way and cuts every hazard's weight most for the earliest years.

A multiplier on the after rate is the wrong shape. The ratio of transition to after rates runs from 1.4 to 100 across hazards, places and ends of the range, so one factor per hazard overshoots somewhere unless it is set by the smallest ratio, as I did. A rate of after + (transition - after) x s(L), with s = 0.4, 0.15 and 0 at leads of 1, 3 and 5 or more years, says what I mean and needs three numbers.

Existential risk with a short lead. The model spreads the chance evenly over the five turbulent years, including those before 2027; for automation in 2028 or 2029 that places 60% to 80% of it in the past. It should be spread over the turbulent years still ahead. And the factor should act on the odds, not the probability: 0.8 x 1.6 is capped at 1.

The turbulent period is five years at every lead time, but its true length grows with the lead: one to three years if automation comes by 2030, perhaps eight to fifteen if it comes after 2045. My factors at long leads include that dilution (about 0.9, 0.78, 0.65, 0.57 at 8, 12, 20 and 30 years). If the model were given a length that depends on the lead, they should be divided by those figures.

Long leads leave out two near-term risks. Sentinel's forecasts (33% for a week-long OECD outage by the end of 2028) assume no AGI, so cyber risk may keep rising through the late 2020s whatever the year of automation; the model holds today's rate until the run-up. And a reader whose year is later than markets expect faces the bust of the 2026 AI debt boom in the next few years.

The reference differs by hazard: about 4 to 5 years for cyber and bio, 5 to 6 for the economy, 5 to 7 for war, 8 to 12 for the existential figure. Only the last is reflected in the table. Raising pExistential to about 0.23 and setting its factor to 1 at five years would be equivalent and perhaps clearer.

The factors do not vary by place. Buenos Aires meets war and nuclear risk only indirectly, and its utilities and banks are the trailing-edge defenders for whom lead time helps latest; its cyber factors probably fall more slowly beyond eight years than the table says.

Whether longer timelines mean a slower takeoff is disputed: Davidson and MacAskill and Taylor say yes, Kokotajlo that a compute overhang could make a late takeoff very fast. If he is right the factors at 12 to 30 years should sit near 1; only my high ends allow for it.

Because all AI figures share one draw, the low end of each factor is paired with the sceptic's rates and the high end with the highly concerned view. I oriented the ranges for that (beyond five years, low means that defenders adapt quickly given time), but the pairing was not part of the brief.

No forecaster has been asked the question the model needs. A small panel (Sentinel, Samotsvety, FRI) could answer it directly: the yearly chance of a week-long outage, a banking crisis or a great-power war in the five years before full automation, given automation in 2030, 2035 and 2045.
